options.a: Lower credit risk and usually higher yields
options.b: Higher credit risk and usually higher yields
options.c: Lower credit risk and usually lower yields
options.d: Equal credit risk but longer maturities

distractorExplanations.b: Higher credit risk and yields describe junk (high-yield) bonds.
distractorExplanations.d: Ratings reflect different credit risk; maturity is not the distinction.
distractorExplanations.a: Investors accept lower yields for lower credit risk, not higher.

options.a: Semiannual coupon payments at a fixed rate
options.b: Interest paid in a lump sum each year
options.c: Price gains from falling rates only
options.d: Accretion from discount to face value

distractorExplanations.a: Zero-coupon bonds pay no periodic coupons.
distractorExplanations.b: Zeros make no annual payments; all return comes at maturity or sale.
distractorExplanations.c: Rate changes affect price, but the built-in return is the accreting discount.

options.a: Mortgage loans insured by federal agencies
options.b: Construction loans made to homebuilders
options.c: Direct ownership of a single rental property
options.d: Real estate cash flows via a pooled security

distractorExplanations.a: Agency-insured mortgages describe GNMA pass-throughs, not REITs.
distractorExplanations.c: REIT holders own shares in a portfolio, not title to a property.
distractorExplanations.b: Some mortgage REITs lend, but REITs mainly give pooled real estate exposure.

options.a: Has voting rights but is paid after common holders
options.b: Gets dividend priority over common, with limited votes
options.c: Pays variable dividends that rise with earnings
options.d: Has priority over bonds in a corporate liquidation

distractorExplanations.c: Preferred dividends are usually fixed; common dividends vary with earnings.
distractorExplanations.d: Bondholders are paid before preferred holders in liquidation.
distractorExplanations.a: Preferred holders are paid before common and usually cannot vote.

options.a: Long-term, investment-grade corporate notes
options.b: Short-term, high-quality debt instruments
options.c: Short-term, high-yield corporate bonds
options.d: Exchange-traded funds holding T-notes

distractorExplanations.c: Money market instruments are high quality; high-yield debt is not.
distractorExplanations.d: An ETF is a fund, not a money market instrument, and T-notes run 2–10 years.
distractorExplanations.a: Long-term notes are capital-market instruments; money market paper matures within about a year.

options.a: Interest taxed at long-term capital gain rates
options.b: Capital gains exempt from all federal taxes
options.c: Principal guaranteed by the issuing state
options.d: Interest often exempt from federal income tax

distractorExplanations.b: Gains on municipal bonds are taxable; only the interest is usually exempt.
distractorExplanations.c: Munis carry credit risk; states do not guarantee local issuers' principal.
distractorExplanations.a: Taxable municipal interest is taxed as ordinary income, and most muni interest is federally exempt.

options.a: The insurer, through its general account
options.b: The separate account's portfolio manager
options.c: The contract owner, through subaccounts
options.d: The insurer for all subaccount losses

distractorExplanations.a: General-account guarantees back fixed annuities, not variable subaccount returns.
distractorExplanations.b: Managers run the subaccounts but do not absorb investment losses.
distractorExplanations.d: The insurer bears investment risk only on fixed or guaranteed riders, not subaccount returns.

options.a: Bond price sensitivity to rate changes
options.b: Time remaining until a bond matures
options.c: A stock's sensitivity to the market
options.d: Credit risk of a bond's issuer

distractorExplanations.b: Maturity is a date; duration weights the timing of all cash flows.
distractorExplanations.c: Sensitivity of a stock to the market is beta.
distractorExplanations.d: Credit risk is measured by ratings and spreads, not duration.

options.a: A foreign share traded on its home exchange
options.b: A U.S. company's shares sold to foreign buyers
options.c: A U.S.-traded receipt for foreign company shares
options.d: A fund that holds a basket of foreign stocks

distractorExplanations.a: An ADR trades in the U.S., not on the foreign home exchange.
distractorExplanations.b: ADRs represent foreign issuers' shares, not U.S. companies'.
distractorExplanations.d: A basket of foreign stocks is a fund, while an ADR represents one issuer.

options.a: Reinvestment risk if called when rates fall
options.b: Default risk if called when rates rise
options.c: Liquidity risk because they cannot be sold
options.d: Inflation risk because coupons adjust to CPI

distractorExplanations.b: Issuers call bonds when rates fall, not when they rise, and calling is not default.
distractorExplanations.c: Callable bonds trade in the secondary market like other bonds.
distractorExplanations.d: Callable bond coupons are fixed; CPI-adjusted coupons describe TIPS.

options.a: Flexible strategies, higher fees, and investor eligibility limits
options.b: Lower fees and restrictions on leverage and short selling
options.c: Daily liquidity and SEC registration as investment companies
options.d: Open availability to retail investors with low investment minimums

distractorExplanations.b: Hedge funds typically charge more and may use leverage and shorting freely.
distractorExplanations.d: Hedge funds are usually limited to accredited or qualified investors with high minimums.
distractorExplanations.c: Hedge funds usually limit redemptions and rely on exemptions from Investment Company Act registration.

options.a: Direct voting control over each underlying stock
options.b: Guaranteed principal backed by the fund sponsor
options.c: Intraday trading at prices set by the market
options.d: Professional management and diversification

distractorExplanations.b: Mutual funds do not guarantee principal; share values fluctuate.
distractorExplanations.c: Mutual funds are priced once daily at NAV; intraday trading describes ETFs.
distractorExplanations.a: The fund votes proxies for its holdings, not individual shareholders.

options.a: Are priced once a day at net asset value
options.b: Are always actively managed by a portfolio team
options.c: Trade intraday on exchanges at market prices
options.d: Are redeemed directly with the issuing fund

distractorExplanations.a: Once-daily NAV pricing describes open-end mutual funds.
distractorExplanations.d: Retail investors sell ETF shares on an exchange; only authorized participants redeem with the fund.
distractorExplanations.b: Most ETFs track indexes; active ETFs exist but are not the rule.

options.a: Rising interest rates lowering prices
options.b: Inflation eroding purchasing power
options.c: Reinvestment of coupons at lower rates
options.d: Default by the U.S. Treasury as issuer

distractorExplanations.a: TIPS prices still fall when real rates rise; they do not remove interest-rate risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Reinvestment risk still applies to TIPS coupons.
distractorExplanations.d: Default risk on Treasuries is minimal; TIPS are designed for inflation.

options.a: Buy the stock at the strike before expiration
options.b: Sell the stock at the strike before expiration
options.c: Buy the stock at the strike only at expiration
options.d: Sell the stock at market price at expiration

distractorExplanations.c: Exercise only at expiration describes European-style options.
distractorExplanations.d: A call gives a right to buy at the strike, not to sell at market.
distractorExplanations.b: The right to sell at the strike belongs to a put buyer.

options.a: A mostly bond portfolio to protect principal
options.b: Equal weights in stocks, bonds, and cash
options.c: A higher equity allocation than a retiree
options.d: Mostly money market funds for liquidity

distractorExplanations.a: A long horizon and high tolerance allow more equity exposure.
distractorExplanations.b: An equal split is more conservative than this profile needs.
distractorExplanations.d: Heavy cash sacrifices growth over a long horizon.

options.a: Municipal bonds inside a traditional IRA
options.b: Tax-efficient index funds in tax-deferred accounts
options.c: High-yield bonds in a taxable brokerage account
options.d: Tax-inefficient assets in tax-advantaged accounts

distractorExplanations.a: Munis are already tax-exempt, so holding them in an IRA wastes the benefit.
distractorExplanations.b: Tax-efficient index funds usually belong in taxable accounts.
distractorExplanations.c: High-yield bond interest is taxed as ordinary income, so it fits better in tax-advantaged accounts.

options.a: Roth IRAs of the original owner after age 73
options.b: Traditional IRAs and 401(k)s after RMD age
options.c: 529 plans once the beneficiary turns 18
options.d: Taxable brokerage accounts after retirement

distractorExplanations.a: Original Roth IRA owners have no RMDs.
distractorExplanations.c: 529 plans have no required distributions.
distractorExplanations.d: Taxable accounts have no required distributions.

options.a: Investing a lump sum when prices look low
options.b: Buying the same number of shares each month
options.c: Selling a fixed dollar amount each month
options.d: Investing a fixed dollar amount at intervals

distractorExplanations.a: Buying on perceived lows is market timing.
distractorExplanations.b: A fixed share count is not dollar-cost averaging; the dollar amount is fixed.
distractorExplanations.c: Fixed withdrawals are a systematic withdrawal plan.

options.a: Growth stocks for a higher expected return
options.b: Long-term bonds to lock in a higher yield
options.c: A balanced fund of stocks and bonds
options.d: Capital preservation and liquidity

distractorExplanations.a: Stocks can fall sharply within a year.
distractorExplanations.b: Long bonds can lose value if rates rise before the purchase.
distractorExplanations.c: A balanced fund still carries meaningful equity risk over 12 months.

options.a: Reduce unsystematic risk through low correlation
options.b: Remove market risk by holding many securities
options.c: Raise expected return without adding risk
options.d: Replace the need to set an asset allocation

distractorExplanations.b: Market (systematic) risk cannot be diversified away.
distractorExplanations.c: Diversification improves risk-adjusted return but does not raise return for free.
distractorExplanations.d: Diversification works within an allocation; it does not replace one.

options.a: The client's age as the single deciding factor
options.b: The client's past returns in other accounts
options.c: The risk level of the adviser's model portfolio
options.d: Willingness and ability to take risk, plus goals

distractorExplanations.a: Age matters, but it is only one input.
distractorExplanations.b: Past returns do not show willingness or capacity to bear losses.
distractorExplanations.c: The model's risk describes the product, not the client.

series-6-readiness-check-suitability-011.prompt: When assessing a client's risk tolerance, an adviser should consider:

options.a: Everyone pays the same percentage of income
options.b: Tax rates fall as taxable income rises
options.c: Taxes are based on spending, not income
options.d: Marginal rates rise as taxable income rises

distractorExplanations.a: One rate for all income levels is a flat tax.
distractorExplanations.b: Falling rates as income rises is a regressive system.
distractorExplanations.c: Taxes on spending are consumption taxes, such as sales taxes.

options.a: Buys more of the best performers to add momentum
options.b: Changes target weights to follow market trends
options.c: Sells winners and buys laggards to reset targets
options.d: Moves the full portfolio to cash after losses

distractorExplanations.a: Adding to winners increases drift from targets, the opposite of rebalancing.
distractorExplanations.b: Rebalancing restores existing targets; it does not chase trends.
distractorExplanations.d: Moving to cash after losses is market timing, not rebalancing.

options.a: Hold winning positions too long before selling
options.b: Overweight recent news when forecasting prices
options.c: Feel losses more strongly than equal gains
options.d: Anchor to the price they originally paid

distractorExplanations.a: Loss aversion leads investors to sell winners early and hold losers.
distractorExplanations.d: Fixing on a purchase price is anchoring.
distractorExplanations.b: Overweighting recent events is recency bias.

options.a: Actively managed funds with high turnover
options.b: Low-turnover index equity funds
options.c: Taxable bond funds paying monthly interest
options.d: Short-term trading to harvest small gains

distractorExplanations.a: High turnover generates frequent taxable capital gains distributions.
distractorExplanations.d: Short-term gains are taxed at higher ordinary income rates.
distractorExplanations.c: Bond interest is taxed as ordinary income each year.

options.a: Disclosure, suitability, pricing, and supervision
options.b: Disclosure, care, conflict of interest, compliance
options.c: Know your customer, care, fair pricing, and loyalty
options.d: Disclosure, best execution, suitability, and training

distractorExplanations.a: Reg BI's components are disclosure, care, conflict of interest, and compliance; pricing is not one of them.
distractorExplanations.c: Fair pricing and loyalty are not the named Reg BI obligations.
distractorExplanations.d: Best execution and training are separate FINRA duties, not Reg BI components.

series-6-readiness-check-suitability-001.prompt: Regulation Best Interest is built on which four component obligations?
series-6-readiness-check-suitability-001.explanation: Reg BI requires broker-dealers to meet a disclosure obligation, a care obligation, a conflict-of-interest obligation, and a compliance obligation when recommending securities to retail customers.

options.a: Buying just under a breakpoint to save the client money
options.b: Telling clients about breakpoints in the fund prospectus
options.c: Selling just below a breakpoint to earn a higher charge
options.d: Combining family accounts to reach a lower sales charge

distractorExplanations.a: The violation is failing to help the client reach a discount, not saving them money.
distractorExplanations.b: Disclosing breakpoints is required and proper.
distractorExplanations.d: Combining eligible family accounts is a legitimate way to reach breakpoints.

series-6-readiness-check-suitability-002.prompt: Breakpoint selling, which FINRA prohibits, means:
series-6-readiness-check-suitability-002.explanation: Breakpoint selling is recommending a purchase just below a breakpoint, or splitting purchases across fund families, so the customer pays a higher sales charge and the representative earns more.

options.a: Up to 13 months, and it can be backdated 90 days
options.b: Up to 12 months, and it cannot be backdated
options.c: Up to 24 months, and it can be backdated 30 days
options.d: Up to 6 months, and it can be backdated 60 days

distractorExplanations.b: The standard LOI window is 13 months, and it can be backdated up to 90 days.
distractorExplanations.c: 24 months is too long; the window is 13 months.
distractorExplanations.d: Six months is too short; the window is 13 months with a 90-day backdate.

series-6-readiness-check-suitability-007.prompt: A letter of intent (LOI) for mutual fund breakpoints typically covers:
series-6-readiness-check-suitability-007.explanation: A letter of intent lets a customer receive a breakpoint discount now by promising to invest the breakpoint amount within 13 months. It may be backdated up to 90 days to cover a recent purchase.

options.a: At the NAV calculated at the prior day's close
options.b: At the next NAV calculated after the order arrives
options.c: At the NAV in effect when the client signs the form
options.d: At the average NAV over the previous five trading days

distractorExplanations.a: Using a prior NAV is backward pricing, which the 1940 Act rules prohibit.
distractorExplanations.c: Signing a form does not set the price; receipt of the order does.
distractorExplanations.d: There is no averaging; each order gets the next computed NAV.

series-6-readiness-check-regulations-001.prompt: Under forward pricing, a mutual fund order is filled:
series-6-readiness-check-regulations-001.explanation: Rule 22c-1 requires forward pricing: purchase and redemption orders are priced at the next net asset value computed after the fund or its agent receives the order, usually at the 4 p.m. ET close.

options.a: Within 3 business days of the redemption request
options.b: Within 7 calendar days of the redemption request
options.c: Within 30 days of the redemption request
options.d: Within one business day of the redemption request

distractorExplanations.a: Three business days is not the 1940 Act redemption standard.
distractorExplanations.c: Thirty days is far longer than the Act allows.
distractorExplanations.d: Many funds pay next day, but the legal outer limit is seven days.

series-6-readiness-check-regulations-002.prompt: Under the Investment Company Act of 1940, a mutual fund must generally pay redemption proceeds:
series-6-readiness-check-regulations-002.explanation: Section 22(e) of the Investment Company Act generally requires open-end funds to pay redemption proceeds within seven calendar days, except in limited emergencies permitted by the SEC.

options.a: 5.75% of the public offering price
options.b: 8.5% of the net asset value
options.c: 8.5% of the public offering price
options.d: 10% of the public offering price

distractorExplanations.a: 5.75% is a common equity fund load, not the FINRA maximum.
distractorExplanations.b: The cap is measured against the public offering price, not NAV.
distractorExplanations.d: 10% exceeds the FINRA maximum sales charge.

series-6-readiness-check-regulations-003.prompt: Under FINRA rules, the maximum sales charge on a mutual fund purchase is:
series-6-readiness-check-regulations-003.explanation: FINRA caps mutual fund sales charges at 8.5% of the public offering price. Funds that do not offer breakpoints, rights of accumulation, or reinvestment at NAV must charge less.

options.a: Only after the customer's first trade settles
options.b: Within 30 days after the account is opened
options.c: At or before the recommendation, order, or account
options.d: Only when the customer asks about firm conflicts

distractorExplanations.a: Form CRS must be delivered before or at the first key event, not after settlement.
distractorExplanations.b: Delivery after account opening is too late.
distractorExplanations.d: Delivery is required to all retail investors, not only on request.

series-6-readiness-check-regulations-004.prompt: A broker-dealer must deliver Form CRS to a new retail investor:
series-6-readiness-check-regulations-004.explanation: Form CRS must be delivered before or at the earliest of a recommendation, placing an order, or opening an account for a retail investor.

options.a: Within 10 days of the event occurring
options.b: Within 60 days of the event
options.c: At the next annual registration renewal
options.d: Within 30 days of learning of it

distractorExplanations.a: Ten days is not the Form U4 amendment deadline.
distractorExplanations.b: Sixty days is too long for U4 amendments.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting for renewal would leave the record inaccurate for months.

series-6-readiness-check-regulations-005.prompt: A registered representative's Form U4 must generally be amended for a reportable event:
series-6-readiness-check-regulations-005.explanation: Firms must keep Form U4 current. Reportable events such as certain liens, judgments, or regulatory actions generally must be amended within 30 days of the firm learning of them.

options.a: No notice if the activity is unrelated to securities
options.b: Prior written notice to the member firm
options.c: Written notice to FINRA within 30 days
options.d: Approval from the state securities administrator

distractorExplanations.a: Rule 3270 applies to outside business activities even if unrelated to securities.
distractorExplanations.c: Notice goes to the member firm, not directly to FINRA.
distractorExplanations.d: Outside business activities are a firm notice issue, not state approval.

series-6-readiness-check-regulations-006.prompt: Under FINRA Rule 3270, a representative who starts a paid outside business activity must give:
series-6-readiness-check-regulations-006.explanation: FINRA Rule 3270 requires registered persons to give their member firm prior written notice before engaging in outside business activities for compensation, so the firm can assess conflicts.

options.a: Up to $500,000, including $250,000 in cash
options.b: Up to $250,000, including $100,000 in cash
options.c: Up to $500,000 for market losses on securities
options.d: Unlimited protection for securities held

distractorExplanations.b: These are not SIPC's limits; the cap is $500,000 with a $250,000 cash sublimit.
distractorExplanations.c: SIPC never covers market losses; it replaces missing assets at a failed firm.
distractorExplanations.d: SIPC protection is capped, not unlimited.

series-6-readiness-check-regulations-007.prompt: SIPC protects each customer of a failed broker-dealer for:
series-6-readiness-check-regulations-007.explanation: SIPC restores missing customer cash and securities up to $500,000 per customer, including up to $250,000 in cash. It does not protect against market losses.

options.a: Over $10,000 in cash
options.b: Over $5,000 in cash
options.c: Over $3,000 in cash
options.d: Over $25,000 in cash

distractorExplanations.b: $5,000 is the broker-dealer SAR threshold, not the CTR threshold.
distractorExplanations.c: $3,000 relates to recordkeeping for money orders and wires, not CTRs.
distractorExplanations.d: $25,000 is not the currency transaction threshold.

series-6-readiness-check-regulations-008.prompt: A broker-dealer must file a Currency Transaction Report (CTR) for a customer transaction involving:
series-6-readiness-check-regulations-008.explanation: Firms must file a CTR with FinCEN for cash transactions over $10,000 in one business day, including multiple related transactions that total more than $10,000.

options.a: At least 25% of its directors
options.b: At least 40% of its directors
options.c: At least 75% of its directors
options.d: All of its directors

distractorExplanations.a: 25% is below the 1940 Act minimum.
distractorExplanations.c: Many funds exceed 75% by practice, but the statutory floor is 40%.
distractorExplanations.d: Interested directors, such as adviser officers, may serve on the board.

series-6-readiness-check-regulations-009.prompt: Under the Investment Company Act of 1940, a mutual fund board must have independent (non-interested) directors making up:
series-6-readiness-check-regulations-009.explanation: The Investment Company Act requires that at least 40% of a fund's board be independent of the adviser and underwriter. Many funds exceed this through exemptive rules or best practice.

options.a: Buying fund shares just before the ex-dividend date
options.b: Placing orders just before the 4 p.m. market close
options.c: Switching between funds in the same family
options.d: Accepting orders after 4 p.m. at that day's NAV

distractorExplanations.a: Buying before ex-dividend is legal, though often unwise for taxes.
distractorExplanations.b: Orders received before the close properly get that day's NAV.
distractorExplanations.c: Exchanges within a family are legal if not abusive market timing.

series-6-readiness-check-regulations-010.prompt: Late trading in mutual funds, which is illegal, means:
series-6-readiness-check-regulations-010.explanation: Late trading lets some investors place orders after the 4 p.m. close but receive that day's NAV, exploiting news released after the close. It violates forward pricing rules.

options.a: Monthly, whether or not there was activity
options.b: Annually, together with the tax forms
options.c: Only in months with trading activity
options.d: At least quarterly

distractorExplanations.a: Monthly statements are required only in months with activity, not always.
distractorExplanations.b: Annual statements are too infrequent under FINRA rules.
distractorExplanations.c: Statements are still due at least quarterly even without activity.

series-6-readiness-check-regulations-011.prompt: FINRA Rule 2231 requires broker-dealers to send customer account statements:
series-6-readiness-check-regulations-011.explanation: FINRA Rule 2231 requires customer account statements at least once each calendar quarter, showing positions, money balances, and account activity.

options.a: Suspicious transactions of $10,000 or more
options.b: Suspicious transactions of $2,000 or more
options.c: Suspicious transactions of $5,000 or more
options.d: Any cash deposit, regardless of amount

distractorExplanations.a: $10,000 is the CTR threshold, not the broker-dealer SAR threshold.
distractorExplanations.b: $2,000 is the money services business SAR threshold, not the broker-dealer threshold.
distractorExplanations.d: SARs are based on suspicion and a threshold, not every cash deposit.

series-6-readiness-check-regulations-012.prompt: Broker-dealers must file a Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) for:
series-6-readiness-check-regulations-012.explanation: Broker-dealers must file a SAR within 30 days for transactions of $5,000 or more that they know or suspect involve illegal funds, evasion, or no apparent lawful purpose.

options.a: Changing the fund's investment objective
options.b: Hiring a new portfolio manager at the adviser
options.c: Changing the fund's transfer agent
options.d: Declaring the fund's annual dividend

distractorExplanations.b: Staffing at the adviser is a management decision, not a shareholder vote.
distractorExplanations.c: Service providers such as transfer agents are chosen by the board.
distractorExplanations.d: Dividends are declared by the board.

series-6-readiness-check-regulations-013.prompt: Which change requires a mutual fund shareholder vote?
series-6-readiness-check-regulations-013.explanation: Under the Investment Company Act, shareholders vote on changes to fundamental investment objectives or policies, on new advisory contracts, and on electing directors.

options.a: More than 10 retail investors in 30 days
options.b: More than 25 retail investors in 30 days
options.c: More than 50 retail investors in 90 days
options.d: More than 100 retail investors in a year

distractorExplanations.a: Ten is not the Rule 2210 threshold.
distractorExplanations.c: The threshold is 25 retail investors within 30 days.
distractorExplanations.d: The rule uses a 30-day window and 25 investors.

series-6-readiness-check-regulations-014.prompt: Under FINRA Rule 2210, a written communication becomes a retail communication when it goes to:
series-6-readiness-check-regulations-014.explanation: A retail communication is written material distributed to more than 25 retail investors within any 30-day period. Communications to 25 or fewer are correspondence.

options.a: Monthly
options.b: Quarterly
options.c: Annually only
options.d: Semiannually

distractorExplanations.a: Funds are not required to send monthly shareholder reports.
distractorExplanations.b: Quarterly holdings are filed with the SEC, but shareholder reports go out twice a year.
distractorExplanations.c: Funds must send both an annual and a semiannual report.

series-6-readiness-check-regulations-015.prompt: Mutual funds must send shareholders financial reports at least:
series-6-readiness-check-regulations-015.explanation: Under the Investment Company Act, funds send shareholders reports at least semiannually. The annual report includes audited financial statements.

options.a: Employees fund it through salary deferrals only
options.b: The employer funds it at the same rate for all
options.c: The employer may choose which staff to fund
options.d: Employee and employer contributions must match

distractorExplanations.a: SEP IRAs are funded by employer contributions, not employee deferrals.
distractorExplanations.c: SEP contributions must be the same percentage of pay for all eligible employees.
distractorExplanations.d: There are no employee contributions to match in a SEP.

series-6-readiness-check-retirement-001.prompt: A SEP IRA is characterized by which funding rule?
series-6-readiness-check-retirement-001.explanation: A SEP IRA is funded only by the employer, which must contribute the same percentage of compensation for every eligible employee in any year it contributes.

options.a: No limit on employer size, and a 10% early penalty
options.b: Up to 500 employees, and a 15% early penalty
options.c: Up to 100 employees, and 25% in the first 2 years
options.d: Up to 50 employees, and no early penalty at all

distractorExplanations.a: SIMPLE IRAs are limited to employers with 100 or fewer employees.
distractorExplanations.b: Neither the 500-employee limit nor a 15% penalty applies.
distractorExplanations.d: The limit is 100 employees, and early withdrawals owe a penalty.

series-6-readiness-check-retirement-002.prompt: A SIMPLE IRA is available to employers with how many employees, and what early withdrawal penalty can apply?
series-6-readiness-check-retirement-002.explanation: SIMPLE IRAs are for employers with 100 or fewer employees. Withdrawals within two years of first participation before age 59½ can owe a 25% penalty instead of 10%.

options.a: Taxable as income in the year of conversion
options.b: Tax-free if the owner is over age 59½
options.c: Subject to a 10% penalty on the full amount
options.d: Taxable only when later withdrawn from the Roth

distractorExplanations.b: Age does not make a conversion tax-free; pre-tax amounts are taxed.
distractorExplanations.c: The 10% penalty does not apply to the conversion itself.
distractorExplanations.d: Tax is due in the conversion year, not later.

series-6-readiness-check-retirement-003.prompt: Converting a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA generally makes the pre-tax amount converted:

options.a: Up to 100% of the vested balance with no cap
options.b: The lesser of $50,000 or 50% of the vested balance
options.c: The lesser of $10,000 or 25% of the vested balance
options.d: Only hardship amounts approved by the IRS

distractorExplanations.a: Plan loans are capped; the full balance cannot be borrowed.
distractorExplanations.c: The limits are $50,000 or 50% of vested balance, not these figures.
distractorExplanations.d: Hardship withdrawals are separate from loans and need no IRS approval.

series-6-readiness-check-retirement-004.prompt: If a 401(k) plan allows loans, the maximum is generally:
series-6-readiness-check-retirement-004.explanation: Plan loans are generally limited to the lesser of $50,000 or 50% of the vested balance, with an exception allowing up to $10,000 for small balances. Loans must usually be repaid within five years.

options.a: Private-sector employer retirement plans
options.b: Retirement plans for state employees
options.c: Individual retirement accounts (IRAs)
options.d: Federal government employee plans

distractorExplanations.b: Government plans are exempt from ERISA.
distractorExplanations.c: IRAs are not ERISA employer plans.
distractorExplanations.d: Federal plans are governed by separate statutes, not ERISA.

options.a: The employee bears the investment risk
options.b: The employer promises a set benefit
options.c: Benefits depend on account performance
options.d: Contributions are fixed each year

distractorExplanations.a: Employees bear investment risk in defined contribution plans.
distractorExplanations.c: Performance-based benefits describe defined contribution plans.
distractorExplanations.d: Contributions in a DB plan vary to fund the promised benefit.

series-6-readiness-check-retirement-006.prompt: A defined benefit pension plan is best described as one in which:

options.a: Funded in a trust protected from creditors
options.b: Available on the same terms to all workers
options.c: An unfunded promise open to employer creditors
options.d: Tax-deductible to the employer when promised

distractorExplanations.a: Assets set aside for NQDC remain subject to the employer's creditors.
distractorExplanations.b: Nonqualified plans may favor selected executives.
distractorExplanations.d: The employer deducts the cost when benefits are paid, not when promised.

series-6-readiness-check-retirement-007.prompt: A nonqualified deferred compensation plan is typically:

options.a: Tax-free, since contributions were after-tax
options.b: Taxed at capital gains rates on earnings only
options.c: Taxed as ordinary income, earnings out first
options.d: Taxed pro rata between cost basis and gains

distractorExplanations.a: Earnings on after-tax contributions are still taxable.
distractorExplanations.b: Annuity earnings are taxed as ordinary income, not capital gains.
distractorExplanations.d: Pro rata treatment applies to annuitized payments, not lump-sum withdrawals.

series-6-readiness-check-retirement-008.prompt: Withdrawals from a nonqualified variable annuity before annuitization are generally:
series-6-readiness-check-retirement-008.explanation: Nonqualified annuity withdrawals follow LIFO: earnings come out first and are taxed as ordinary income, with a 10% penalty before age 59½ unless an exception applies.

options.a: Life with period certain
options.b: Joint and last survivor
options.c: Unit refund life annuity
options.d: Straight life only

distractorExplanations.a: A period certain guarantee costs money, so monthly payments are lower.
distractorExplanations.b: Covering two lives lowers each payment.
distractorExplanations.c: A refund feature lowers the monthly amount.

series-6-readiness-check-retirement-009.prompt: Which annuity payout option generally provides the highest monthly payment?
series-6-readiness-check-retirement-009.explanation: Straight life (life only) pays the most per month because payments stop at the annuitant's death, with nothing left for beneficiaries.

options.a: Annuity units
options.b: Accumulation units
options.c: Fund shares at NAV
options.d: Units of a fixed account

distractorExplanations.a: Annuity units are used after annuitization, during payout.
distractorExplanations.c: Owners hold units of subaccounts, not fund shares directly.
distractorExplanations.d: Fixed account values are not measured in variable units.

series-6-readiness-check-retirement-010.prompt: During the accumulation phase, variable annuity purchase payments buy:

options.a: Payments stay the same as the prior month
options.b: Payments fall because the AIR is exceeded
options.c: Payments reset to the original guaranteed amount
options.d: Payments rise for the next period

distractorExplanations.a: Payments change when returns differ from the AIR.
distractorExplanations.b: Returns above the AIR raise payments, not lower them.
distractorExplanations.c: Variable payments are not reset to a guaranteed amount.

series-6-readiness-check-retirement-011.prompt: If separate account returns exceed the assumed interest rate (AIR), variable annuity payments:

options.a: $2,000 a year per beneficiary
options.b: $5,000 a year per beneficiary
options.c: $6,500 a year per contributor
options.d: $18,000 a year per beneficiary

distractorExplanations.b: $5,000 is not the Coverdell limit.
distractorExplanations.c: The limit applies per beneficiary, and $6,500 is not correct.
distractorExplanations.d: $18,000 resembles gift tax exclusion amounts, not the Coverdell limit.

series-6-readiness-check-retirement-012.prompt: Coverdell Education Savings Account contributions are limited to:

options.a: Private for-profit companies of any size
options.b: Self-employed individuals and sole owners
options.c: State and local government employers
options.d: Public schools and 501(c)(3) groups only

distractorExplanations.a: For-profit companies use 401(k) plans, not 457 plans.
distractorExplanations.b: Self-employed people use SEP IRAs or solo 401(k)s.
distractorExplanations.d: Public schools and 501(c)(3) groups use 403(b) plans.

series-6-readiness-check-retirement-013.prompt: Section 457(b) deferred compensation plans are mainly offered by:

options.a: Only if the spouse has some earned income
options.b: Only if both spouses file separate returns
options.c: If the working spouse has enough earned income
options.d: Only if the spouse is at least age 50

distractorExplanations.a: The spousal IRA exists for a spouse without earned income.
distractorExplanations.b: Spousal IRAs require a joint return.
distractorExplanations.d: Age affects catch-up amounts, not eligibility.

series-6-readiness-check-retirement-014.prompt: A non-working spouse may contribute to a spousal IRA:

options.a: Tax-free, since the owner already paid tax
options.b: Income-taxed, with no 10% penalty for heirs
options.c: Taxed at capital gains rates for all heirs
options.d: Income-taxed plus a 10% early penalty

distractorExplanations.a: Pre-tax traditional IRA money is taxed when heirs withdraw it.
distractorExplanations.c: IRA distributions are taxed as ordinary income, not capital gains.
distractorExplanations.d: Beneficiaries are exempt from the 10% early withdrawal penalty.

series-6-readiness-check-retirement-015.prompt: Distributions a beneficiary takes from an inherited traditional IRA are generally:

options.a: On an exchange at prices set by buyers and sellers
options.b: At the prior day's NAV plus any accrued income
options.c: From other shareholders through the fund's transfer agent
options.d: At net asset value through the fund or its agent

distractorExplanations.a: Exchange trading at market prices describes ETFs and closed-end funds.
distractorExplanations.b: Forward pricing uses the next NAV, not the prior day's.
distractorExplanations.c: The fund itself issues and redeems shares; holders do not trade with each other.

options.a: Holds a fixed portfolio and ends on a set date
options.b: Has a board that hires an active portfolio manager
options.c: Trades on an exchange throughout the trading day
options.d: Continuously issues shares to new investors

distractorExplanations.b: UITs have no board or active manager.
distractorExplanations.c: UIT units are usually redeemed with the sponsor, not traded intraday.
distractorExplanations.d: UITs issue units once; continuous issuance describes open-end funds.

options.a: The insurer's general account with a fixed rate
options.b: Separate accounts apart from the general account
options.c: A bank trust account insured by the FDIC
options.d: Guaranteed investment contracts from the insurer

distractorExplanations.a: The general account backs fixed products, not variable subaccounts.
distractorExplanations.c: Separate accounts are not bank accounts and are not FDIC insured.
distractorExplanations.d: GICs are fixed-return contracts, not variable subaccounts.

options.a: A back-end CDSC with higher ongoing 12b-1 fees
options.b: A level load charged each year with no CDSC
options.c: A front-end load with lower ongoing 12b-1 fees
options.d: No sales charge and no 12b-1 fees at all

distractorExplanations.a: A back-end CDSC with higher 12b-1 fees describes Class B shares.
distractorExplanations.b: A level annual charge describes Class C shares.
distractorExplanations.d: No sales charge describes no-load shares, not Class A.

options.a: Portfolio management fees paid to the adviser
options.b: Custody and transfer agent fees for the fund
options.c: Brokerage commissions on portfolio trades
options.d: Marketing and distribution costs

distractorExplanations.a: Management fees are a separate part of the expense ratio.
distractorExplanations.b: Custody and transfer agent costs are other operating expenses.
distractorExplanations.c: Brokerage commissions are not part of the expense ratio at all.

options.a: Lower the sales charge as the purchase grows
options.b: Raise the sales charge as the purchase grows
options.c: Apply only to purchases in a single account
options.d: Waive the sales charge on all reinvestments

distractorExplanations.b: Breakpoints reduce, not increase, the charge on larger purchases.
distractorExplanations.c: Family accounts can often be combined to reach breakpoints.
distractorExplanations.d: Reinvestment at NAV is a separate feature, not a breakpoint.

options.a: Front-end sales loads paid when buying shares
options.b: Management fees and other operating costs
options.c: Brokerage commissions on portfolio trades
options.d: Taxes owed on the fund's distributions

distractorExplanations.a: Sales loads are charged at purchase, outside the expense ratio.
distractorExplanations.c: Trading commissions are not included in the expense ratio.
distractorExplanations.d: Taxes on distributions are paid by shareholders, not the fund.

options.a: Beat its benchmark through active stock picking
options.b: Hold only the ten largest stocks in the market
options.c: Change holdings based on market forecasts
options.d: Track a stated benchmark at low cost

distractorExplanations.a: Beating a benchmark is the goal of active funds.
distractorExplanations.b: Index funds hold the index constituents, not only the largest ten.
distractorExplanations.c: Forecast-driven changes are active management.

options.a: Market price is below the value of its holdings
options.b: Market price is above the value of its holdings
options.c: The fund is charging a sales load on purchases
options.d: The fund must buy back shares at NAV right away

distractorExplanations.b: Price above NAV is a premium, not a discount.
distractorExplanations.c: Discounts reflect market pricing, not sales loads.
distractorExplanations.d: Closed-end funds do not have to redeem shares at NAV.

options.a: Protection from market losses at no added cost
options.b: A guaranteed minimum withdrawal, for a fee
options.c: A higher death benefit paid only to a spouse
options.d: Tax-free withdrawals during the payout phase

distractorExplanations.a: Living benefit riders cost extra.
distractorExplanations.c: Enhanced death benefits are death benefit riders, not living benefits.
distractorExplanations.d: Riders do not change how withdrawals are taxed.

options.a: How often shareholders redeem their shares
options.b: The fund's asset growth over the year
options.c: How often the fund's holdings are traded
options.d: The share of assets held in cash

distractorExplanations.a: Redemption activity is not the turnover ratio.
distractorExplanations.b: Asset growth is a separate statistic.
distractorExplanations.d: Cash allocation is not turnover.

options.a: Recent one-year returns compared with peers
options.b: Star ratings from a fund rating service
options.c: The size of each fund's assets under management
options.d: Expenses, objectives, and prospectus risks

distractorExplanations.a: Short-term returns alone are a weak basis for comparison.
distractorExplanations.b: Ratings are backward-looking and do not replace the prospectus.
distractorExplanations.c: Fund size says little about costs or fit.

series-6-readiness-check-products-028.prompt: When comparing no-load funds, a representative should emphasize:

options.a: Tax-free exchange of one annuity for another
options.b: Tax-free withdrawal of gains after age 59½
options.c: Conversion of an annuity into a Roth IRA
options.d: A rollover of an annuity into a 401(k) plan

distractorExplanations.b: Section 1035 concerns exchanges, not tax-free withdrawals.
distractorExplanations.c: Roth conversions are separate and taxable.
distractorExplanations.d: Section 1035 covers contract-to-contract exchanges, not plan rollovers.

options.a: Individual stocks chosen by a single manager
options.b: Other mutual funds, not direct securities
options.c: Real estate held directly by the fund
options.d: Bank CDs from several insured banks

distractorExplanations.a: A fund of funds holds other funds, not stocks directly.
distractorExplanations.c: Direct real estate is not a fund-of-funds holding.
distractorExplanations.d: Funds of funds do not mainly hold CDs.

options.a: A signed risk disclosure from the customer
options.b: The fund's top rating from a research service
options.c: Approval from the fund's wholesaler
options.d: A reasonable basis and customer-specific fit

distractorExplanations.a: A signature does not replace the representative's suitability analysis.
distractorExplanations.b: Ratings do not show suitability for a specific customer.
distractorExplanations.c: Wholesaler approval is not a suitability requirement.

series-6-readiness-check-suitability-016.prompt: Before recommending a mutual fund, a representative must have:

options.a: Highly volatile sector funds
options.b: Investment-grade bond funds
options.c: Conservative balanced funds
options.d: Money market funds for cash

distractorExplanations.b: Investment-grade bond funds can fit an income-seeking conservative investor.
distractorExplanations.c: Conservative balanced funds may be appropriate.
distractorExplanations.d: Money market funds suit near-term cash needs.

options.a: The commission the representative earns
options.b: Whether a recommended fund fits the goals
options.c: The firm's margin requirements for the account
options.d: The account's eligibility for SIPC coverage

distractorExplanations.a: Commission is not determined by the objective.
distractorExplanations.c: Margin requirements are set by rules, not the objective.
distractorExplanations.d: SIPC eligibility does not depend on objectives.

options.a: Growth funds for higher expected returns
options.b: Long-term bond funds for higher yields
options.c: Principal stability and liquidity
options.d: A variable annuity for tax deferral

distractorExplanations.a: Growth funds can fall sharply in the short term.
distractorExplanations.b: Long-term bond funds lose value when rates rise.
distractorExplanations.d: Annuity surrender charges conflict with near-term needs.

options.a: Choosing the fund with the best past returns
options.b: Setting the customer's investment objective
options.c: Replacing the need to explain fund risks
options.d: Documenting how much volatility fits

distractorExplanations.a: Questionnaires measure the client, not fund performance.
distractorExplanations.b: Objectives are set with the client; the questionnaire is one input.
distractorExplanations.c: Risk disclosure is still required.

options.a: Likely unsuitable without clear documentation
options.b: Suitable if the fund has a strong track record
options.c: Suitable if the customer signs a waiver
options.d: Suitable if the position is under 50% of assets

distractorExplanations.b: Past performance does not make a volatile fund suitable for someone who cannot bear loss.
distractorExplanations.c: Waivers do not cure unsuitable recommendations.
distractorExplanations.d: An arbitrary percentage does not make it suitable.

series-6-readiness-check-suitability-021.prompt: When a customer cannot afford loss of principal, recommending an aggressive growth fund is:

options.a: Tax deductions for annuity contributions
options.b: Surrender charges and limited liquidity
options.c: The annuity's death benefit guarantee
options.d: The insurer's financial strength rating

distractorExplanations.a: Nonqualified annuity contributions are not deductible, but the main issue is liquidity.
distractorExplanations.c: The death benefit does not address a need for cash in two years.
distractorExplanations.d: Insurer strength matters, but it does not solve liquidity needs.

options.a: Guarantees a lower average price per share
options.b: Removes sales charges from each purchase
options.c: May reduce timing risk with fixed amounts
options.d: Protects the account against market losses

distractorExplanations.a: DCA often lowers the average cost, but it does not guarantee it.
distractorExplanations.b: Sales charges still apply to periodic purchases.
distractorExplanations.d: Periodic investing does not protect against losses.

options.a: How the fund's past returns justify the cost
options.b: How the fund's rating compares to its peers
options.c: How higher costs signal better management
options.d: How ongoing costs reduce net returns

distractorExplanations.a: Past returns do not justify future costs.
distractorExplanations.b: Ratings do not explain the cost impact.
distractorExplanations.c: Higher fees do not indicate better management.

options.a: Tax-managed or municipal bond funds
options.b: High-yield corporate bond funds
options.c: Actively traded sector funds
options.d: Real estate investment trust funds

distractorExplanations.b: High-yield bond interest is fully taxable.
distractorExplanations.c: Active trading creates taxable distributions.
distractorExplanations.d: REIT dividends are mostly taxed as ordinary income.

options.a: Which option pays the representative more
options.b: Fees, options, advice, and protections
options.c: Only the investment choices in each
options.d: Only the past returns of each option

distractorExplanations.a: Representative compensation cannot drive the recommendation.
distractorExplanations.c: Investment choices are one factor among several.
distractorExplanations.d: Past returns do not capture fees, services, or protections.

options.a: Separate account values are fully guaranteed
options.b: All riders are included at no extra cost
options.c: Values fluctuate; guarantees may cost extra
options.d: Subaccounts are insured by the FDIC

distractorExplanations.a: Separate account values can decline.
distractorExplanations.b: Riders usually carry extra charges.
distractorExplanations.d: Subaccounts are not FDIC insured.

options.a: Better because B shares have no sales charge
options.b: Better because the CDSC falls over time
options.c: Equal to A shares for any purchase size
options.d: Worse than A shares with breakpoints

distractorExplanations.a: B shares carry a CDSC and higher 12b-1 fees.
distractorExplanations.b: A declining CDSC does not beat A-share breakpoints on large purchases.
distractorExplanations.c: Large purchases often get A-share discounts that B shares lack.

options.a: Unsuitable and a fair dealing violation
options.b: Acceptable within the same fund family
options.c: Acceptable if the client signs off
options.d: Acceptable if the new fund performs better

distractorExplanations.b: Switching to earn commissions is improper even within one family.
distractorExplanations.c: A signature does not cure a commission-driven switch.
distractorExplanations.d: Later performance does not justify switching for commissions.

options.a: Use the more aggressive spouse's profile
options.b: Document both profiles and the joint goal
options.c: Use the more conservative spouse's profile
options.d: Open separate accounts without discussion

distractorExplanations.a: Ignoring one owner's profile risks unsuitable advice.
distractorExplanations.c: Defaulting to one owner ignores the joint objective.
distractorExplanations.d: Splitting accounts without discussing goals skips the analysis.

options.a: Broker-dealer registration and net capital rules
options.b: Public offerings of new corporate securities
options.c: Trading on national securities exchanges and OTC
options.d: Mutual funds, UITs, and other investment companies

distractorExplanations.a: Broker-dealer registration falls under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.
distractorExplanations.b: Public offerings are governed by the Securities Act of 1933.
distractorExplanations.c: Exchange trading is regulated under the 1934 Act.

options.a: Delivered or made available at or before the sale
options.b: Delivered within 90 days after the purchase date
options.c: Delivered only if the customer asks for a copy
options.d: Delivered only to first-time fund investors

distractorExplanations.b: Delivery after 90 days is too late.
distractorExplanations.c: Delivery is required, not only on request.
distractorExplanations.d: Every purchaser must receive a prospectus.

options.a: Suitability of customer recommendations
options.b: Communications with the public by members
options.c: Outside business activities of representatives
options.d: Customer account statements and confirmations

distractorExplanations.a: Suitability is Rule 2111.
distractorExplanations.c: Outside business activities fall under Rule 3270.
distractorExplanations.d: Account statements are Rule 2231.

options.a: The representative's personal account balances
options.b: The firm's commission schedule for the rep
options.c: Registrations, exams, and disclosure events
options.d: Customer complaints only after arbitration

distractorExplanations.a: Personal balances are not CRD data.
distractorExplanations.b: Commission schedules are not part of CRD.
distractorExplanations.d: CRD includes reportable complaints, not only arbitrated ones.

options.a: Only state insurance rules, since 529s are not securities
options.b: No prospectus, since the state sponsors the plan
options.c: Only MSRB approval of each individual sale
options.d: Securities rules and plan disclosure documents

distractorExplanations.a: 529 plans are municipal fund securities under securities rules.
distractorExplanations.b: 529 plans provide an offering document that must be delivered.
distractorExplanations.c: MSRB rules apply, but they do not require approval of each sale.

options.a: Content is fair, balanced, and not misleading
options.b: Content is approved by FINRA before its use
options.c: Content includes a guarantee of performance
options.d: Content is filed with the SEC before its use

distractorExplanations.b: Principal approval is internal; FINRA filing is separate.
distractorExplanations.c: Performance guarantees are prohibited.
distractorExplanations.d: Retail communications are not filed with the SEC for approval.

options.a: Show returns since the fund's best year
options.b: Include standard periods and expenses
options.c: Show only gross returns before fees
options.d: Include a projected future return

distractorExplanations.a: Choosing a favorable start date is cherry-picking.
distractorExplanations.c: Fee disclosure is required for fair presentation.
distractorExplanations.d: Projections of fund performance are generally prohibited.

options.a: Respond only if the complaint is in writing
options.b: Refer the customer directly to FINRA
options.c: Close the account to end the dispute
options.d: Log, supervise, and respond per procedures

distractorExplanations.a: Firms must handle complaints under procedures, and written complaints must be recorded.
distractorExplanations.b: Firms must handle complaints themselves.
distractorExplanations.c: Closing the account does not resolve the firm's obligations.

options.a: Registration or notice filing in the state
options.b: Full merit review of each fund offered
options.c: Approval of each sale by the administrator
options.d: No filing, since funds are federal covered

distractorExplanations.b: Mutual funds are federal covered and not subject to state merit review.
distractorExplanations.c: States do not approve individual sales.
distractorExplanations.d: States may still require notice filings and fees.

options.a: Filing a report for every wire transfer
options.b: Customer identification and monitoring
options.c: Refusing all cash deposits from customers
options.d: Annual audits by FinCEN of every firm

distractorExplanations.a: Not every wire requires a report.
distractorExplanations.c: Firms may accept cash with reporting rules.
distractorExplanations.d: FinCEN does not audit every firm annually.

options.a: Moves with the rep if customers agree verbally
options.b: Is shared between the old and new firm
options.c: Stays with the firm; improper use is barred
options.d: Is deleted once the rep leaves the firm

distractorExplanations.a: Customer records belong to the firm, not the representative.
distractorExplanations.b: Firms do not split customer records.
distractorExplanations.d: Records must be retained, not deleted.

options.a: Allowed without limit if disclosed
options.b: Allowed if under $500 per person
options.c: Allowed if paid by the fund itself
options.d: Supervised and limited by rule

distractorExplanations.a: FINRA limits gifts; disclosure alone is not enough.
distractorExplanations.b: FINRA Rule 3220 sets a much lower annual per-person limit, and firm approval rules still apply.
distractorExplanations.c: Who pays does not remove the limit.

series-6-readiness-check-regulations-028.prompt: Under FINRA rules, gifts to associated persons from fund vendors above the threshold:

options.a: Follow correction and disclosure procedures
options.b: Correct errors only above a set dollar amount
options.c: Pass the cost of the error to shareholders
options.d: Correct the error at the next audit date

distractorExplanations.b: Funds have materiality policies, but they still follow procedures for every error.
distractorExplanations.c: Shareholders should not bear the fund's errors.
distractorExplanations.d: Correction must be prompt, not at the next audit.

options.a: Allowed with no special rules
options.b: Subject to margin and suitability rules
options.c: Allowed only in retirement accounts
options.d: Allowed if shares are held over a year

distractorExplanations.a: Margin rules and suitability still apply.
distractorExplanations.c: Margin is not allowed in retirement accounts.
distractorExplanations.d: Holding period does not govern margin use.

options.a: Deductible for everyone regardless of income
options.b: Never deductible under current tax law
options.c: Deductible only for those without a job
options.d: Deductible within IRS limits if eligible

distractorExplanations.a: Deductibility phases out for workplace plan participants above income limits.
distractorExplanations.b: Many taxpayers can deduct traditional IRA contributions.
distractorExplanations.c: Earned income is required to contribute.

options.a: Tax-free if age and holding rules are met
options.b: Taxed as ordinary income on earnings
options.c: Taxed at capital gains rates on earnings
options.d: Tax-free only if taken before age 59½

distractorExplanations.b: Qualified Roth withdrawals are tax-free.
distractorExplanations.c: Roth earnings are not taxed as gains when qualified.
distractorExplanations.d: Qualified withdrawals generally require age 59½ or another qualifying event.

options.a: Immediately, in every plan
options.b: Per the plan's vesting schedule
options.c: Only after ten years of service
options.d: Only when the employee retires

distractorExplanations.a: Some plans vest immediately, but many use schedules.
distractorExplanations.c: Vesting schedules cannot exceed ERISA maximums, which are shorter.
distractorExplanations.d: Vesting is based on service, not retirement.

options.a: At age 59½ for all IRA owners
options.b: At age 65, alongside Medicare
options.c: At the IRS-required age by law
options.d: At age 70½ for all IRA owners

distractorExplanations.a: Age 59½ ends the early withdrawal penalty; it does not start RMDs.
distractorExplanations.b: RMD age is not tied to Medicare eligibility.
distractorExplanations.d: 70½ was the old rule; the SECURE Acts raised the age.

options.a: Keeps the same allocation until the target date
options.b: Guarantees the balance at the target date
options.c: Grows more aggressive as the date nears
options.d: Becomes more conservative over time

distractorExplanations.a: Target-date funds follow a glide path that changes over time.
distractorExplanations.b: Target-date funds do not guarantee values.
distractorExplanations.c: They become more conservative, not more aggressive.

options.a: Income tax plus a 10% penalty, unless exempt
options.b: Income tax only, with no additional penalty
options.c: Capital gains tax plus a 10% penalty on gains
options.d: A 25% penalty with no income tax due

distractorExplanations.b: Early withdrawals usually add a 10% penalty.
distractorExplanations.c: IRA withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income, not capital gains.
distractorExplanations.d: The 25% rate applies to early SIMPLE withdrawals in the first two years.

options.a: Allows contributions above annual IRS limits
options.b: Keeps tax deferral if done as a direct rollover
options.c: Converts pre-tax money into Roth money tax-free
options.d: Gives the assets FDIC insurance in the IRA

distractorExplanations.a: Rollovers do not change annual contribution limits.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving pre-tax money to a Roth is a taxable conversion.
distractorExplanations.d: IRA investments are not FDIC insured unless held in bank deposits.

options.a: Contribute without any annual dollar limit
options.b: Skip the plan's vesting schedule
options.c: Add more above standard limits after age 50
options.d: Make Roth contributions above income limits

distractorExplanations.a: Catch-up contributions have their own limits.
distractorExplanations.b: Catch-ups do not affect vesting.
distractorExplanations.d: Catch-ups do not waive Roth IRA income limits.

options.a: Designed to replace all pre-retirement income
options.b: Tax-free for every recipient at any income
options.c: Available in full at age 62 for all workers
options.d: Based on earnings and claiming age

distractorExplanations.a: Social Security replaces only part of income.
distractorExplanations.b: Up to 85% of benefits can be taxable.
distractorExplanations.c: Claiming at 62 permanently reduces benefits.

options.a: Transfers to charity that can count toward RMDs
options.b: Unlimited tax-free gifts to any private foundation
options.c: Deductions for charitable gifts from any account
options.d: Withdrawals for any purpose without taxes

distractorExplanations.b: QCDs have annual limits, and private foundations generally do not qualify.
distractorExplanations.c: QCDs come from IRAs and are excluded from income, not deducted.
distractorExplanations.d: Only direct transfers to qualifying charities receive QCD treatment.

options.a: A required lump-sum payout within one year
options.b: A spousal rollover others cannot choose
options.c: An exemption from all income taxes
options.d: A transfer into a 529 plan for heirs

distractorExplanations.a: Spouses are not forced into a lump-sum payout.
distractorExplanations.c: Distributions are still taxable.
